title: Lecture 3 – Binocular vision & strabismus
html:
Source: c3 binocular vision.pptx – 53 slides

Binocular vision #1

Binocular vision #2

  • the ability of the visual cortex
  • to fuse into an unique sensation the two images that the viewed objects build up on both retinas
  • to correctly localize in space these objects.

Components #3

  • Simultaneous perception.
  • simultaneous seeing the two images (similar or dissimilar ) built within each eye
  • In normal binocular vision,
  • both eyes have the same point of fixation,
  • lands on the fovea centralis in each eye.
  • The image of an object always lands on identical areas of the retina
  • corresponding points on the retina.
  • Objects lying on an imaginary circle known as the geometric horopter are projected to these points on the retina.
  • The images of both retinas are therefore identical
  • physiologic diplopia.

Notes: Physiologic diplopia can be demonstrated by placing two vertical pencils in a line along the subject’s visual axis, with the second pencil approximately twice as far from the subject as the first. When the subject focuses on one pencil, the other will appear double.

Components #4

  • Fusing the images
  • perception of only one image from fusion into one of the two images built within each eye.
  • when the images are similar, proper fusion;
  • should dissimilar only an superpositon of the images confusion
  • Only where both retinas convey the same visual impression, (transmit identical images to the brain), will the two retinal images blend into a single perception

Components #5

  • Stereoscopic vision of the fused images.
  • space or 3D vision,
  • overlapping of two a little different images .
  • the two images are not quite identical
  • the two eyes are separated by a distance of 60 mm.
  • each eye sees the object from a different perspective.
  • The brain processes noncorresponding retinal images within Panum’s area into a single 3D visual perception and does not interpret them as double images
  • the brain uses the double images to distinguish differences in depth.

a Geometric horopter. #6

  • The light rays from the fixation point strike the
  • fovea centralis in both eyes in normal simultaneous vision.
  • Therefore, objects A and B on the geometric horopter are projected to corresponding points on the retina.

b Physiologic horopter. #7

  • In a narrow range in front of and behind the horopter(Panum’s area), two retinal images can still be fused into one.
  • Points A and B, which lie outside Panum’s area, are projected to noncorresponding points on the retina.

Conditions for normal binocular vision: #8

  • Anatomical and dioptrical integrity of the eyeballs;
  • Anatomical and functional integrity of the neuromuscular apparatus of the eyeballs
  • intrinsic and extrinsic nerves and muscles ;
  • Functional integrity of both retinas
  • retinal correspondence;
  • both maculas represent normal correspondent retinal points;
  • Normal binocular visual field and central vision.

Methods of examinations #9

  • a)Examining the statical position of both eyes and measuring the strabic deviation by three methods:
  • Cover-test
  • Assessment of corneal light reflex
  • Baren’s prisms

Methods of examinations #10

  • Cover-test
  • Unilateral esotropia of the right eye.
  • Unilateral cover test: When the leading left eye is covered, the deviating right eye adjusts with a movement from medial to lateral and then takes the lead. The covered left eye deviates.
  • When the leading left eye is uncovered again, the right eye reverts to its deviation. The leading left eye is realigned with the fixation point.

Methods of examinations #11

  • Assessment of corneal light reflex
  • The examiner holds a point light source beneath his or her own eyes and observes the light reflections in the patient’s corneas in the near field (40 cm) and at a distance (5m).
  • The reflections are normally in the center of each pupil. If the corneal reflection is not in the center of the pupil in one eye, then a tropia is present in that eye.

Methods of examination #12

  • Baren’s prisms
  • The angle of deviation measured
  • combination
  • cover test
  • the use of prism lens of various refractive powers.

Methods of examinations #13

  • Baren’s prisms
  • The patient fixates on a certain point with the leading eye at a distance of 5m or 30 cm, depending on which angle of deviation is to be measured.
  • The examiner place prism lenses of different refractive power before the patient’s deviant eye until the eye no longer makes any adjustment.
  • the angle of deviation corresponds to the strength of the respective prism and is fully compensated for by that prism.
  • The tip of the prism must always point in the direction of deviation

Methods of examinations #14

  • Baren’s prisms
  • Exact measurement of the angle of deviation
  • the proper prism to compensate for the angle of deviation
  • corrective surgery
  • error lead to undercorrection or overcorrection of the angle of deviation
  • Example:
  • Esotropia of + 15 degrees is corrected by shifting the medial rectus 4.0mm posteriorly and shortening the lateral rectus 5.0mm.

Methods of examinations #15

  • b)Examining the ocular movements
  • the ductions,
  • the versions
  • the vergences

Methods of examinations #16

  • c)Examining the diplopias
  • Hess-Lancaster test

Methods of examinations #17

  • d)Examining binocular vision disturbance
  • synoptophor (the three steps of binocular vision)

Methods of examinations #18

  • e)Examining monocular vision disturbance
  • determining the visual acuity

Disturbances #19

  • eyeball deviations strabismus or squint
  • paralytic or incomitant
  • nonparalytic or concomitant strabismus.

Disturbances #20

  • in every form of strabismus
  • strabic, squiting or deviating eye
  • fixing, nondeviating or straight eye
  • direction of ocular deviation the strabismus
  • Convergent-esotropia,
  • Divergent-exotropia ;
  • Superior-hypertropia
  • Inferior-hypotropia .

Paralytic strabismus #21

  • one or more muscles may be involved
  • Causes
  • anywhere between the muscle and the occipital cortex
  • on the muscle;
  • within the motor nerves (3,4,6);
  • at the nuclei of the motor nerves;
  • at the supranuclear centers;
  • within cortical centers

Paralytic strabismus #22

  • anywhere between the muscle and the occipital cortex
  • The rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (RIMLF)
  • vertical eye movement and phases of rapid nystagmus.
  • The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)
  • horizontal eye movement.

Symptoms #23

  • Diplopia. (double sight)
  • when the eye move in the direction of action of the affected muscle
  • general rule
  • homonymous in a paralysis of an abductor (convergent strabismus)
  • heteronymous in a paralysis of an adductor (divergent strabismus)

Symptoms #24

  • False localization
  • erroneous estimation of the position of an object within the space,
  • consequence of diplopia.
  • Vertigo
  • consequence of diplopia and false localization
  • associated with nausea, vomiting, and faltering gait

Signs #25

  • Eyeball deviation
  • primary deviation
  • the deviation of the paralysed eye when the patient fixes with the straight eye
  • secondary deviation
  • the deviation of the straight eye should the patient fix with the paralysed eye.
  • always greater than that of the deviating one (primary deviation)
  • Limitation of the ocular movements.
  • when the eye moves in the direction of action of the paralysed muscle

Signs #26

  • Angle formed by the optical axes of both eyes.
  • changes in differing positions of the gaze,
  • Marked in the direction of action of the paralysed muscle
  • Vicious posture of the head and work.
  • to avoid diplopia the patient tilts head in the direction of the paralysed muscle, where the muscle is not solicited.
  • When becomes permanent=torticollis

Paralysis variants #27

  • abducens (38%)
  • trochlear (32%)
  • oculomotor (28%)
  • paralysis of associated movements of both eyes
  • convergence, divergence,
  • horizontal parallel movements,
  • vertical parallel movements.
  • paralysis of all muscle=ophthalmoplegia
  • total (intrinsic and extrinsic muscles)
  • external (only extrinsic muscles).

Etiology #28

  • congenital (15%) and acquired.
  • Infections.
  • epidemic encephalitis (tyroid fever, pneumonia),
  • toxiinfections (diphtheria, tetanos),
  • eruptive fever (varicella, measles),
  • influenza, poliomyelitis,
  • multiple sclerosis,
  • herpes, syphilis, tuberculosis;

Etiology #29

  • Exogenous and endogenous poisonings;
  • Vascular lesions
  • meningeal and cerebral hemorrhages,
  • ischemic stroke;
  • Cranioorbital traumatisms,
  • Intracranial tumors
  • by direct compression
  • by intracranial hypertension

Treatment #30

  • etiological
  • antiinflammatory and antibiotic systemically
  • surgical treatment
  • 6-12 months after the paresis

Nonparalytic strabismus (concomitant) #31

  • latent
  • manifest

Latent strabismus ( heterophoria) #32

  • Particularities.
  • Ortophoria (25% of cases)
  • normally no matter of direction of gaze the two eyes are directed that the images of a viewed objects build up on symmetrical retinal regions within each eye.

Latent strabismus ( heterophoria) #33

  • Particularities.
  • Normophoria
  • in most patients the eyes are maintained in normal position by a permanent effort of fusion
  • heterophoria
  • By some individuals this efforts goes to tiredness
  • the muscle balance is disturbed
  • ocular deviations
  • can be suppressed by an additional muscle effort

Latent strabismus ( heterophoria) #34

  • esophoria, deviates nasally,
  • exophoria deviates temporally,
  • hyperphoria (latent elevation) deviates superiorly
  • hypophoria (latent depression) deviation inferiorly.

Latent strabismus ( heterophoria) #35

  • Etiology.
  • refractive errors (hypermetropia, myopia),
  • anomalies of the extrinsic muscles,
  • innervational factors.

Latent strabismus ( heterophoria) #36

  • Management.
  • optical correction of the refractive errors;
  • prismatical glasses with the peak in the direction of the ocular deviation;
  • stereoscopical training in order to consolidate the fusion.

Manifest strabismus #37

  • concomitant strabismus=heterotropia
  • Characteristics
  • arises in childhood,
  • the eye deviation is manifest and permanent
  • both eyes move together without limitation
  • both eyes keep the same anormal relationship between their axes in all gaze directions
  • “concomitant”
  • the movements of the deviating eye are concomitant with those of the straight eye.

Manifest strabismus #38

  • Classification.
  • a) the sense of deviation
  • esotropia (convergent strabismus)
  • deviation nasally;
  • exotropia (divergent strabismus)
  • deviation temporally;
  • Hypertropia
  • superior deviation
  • hypotropia
  • inferior deviation.

Manifest strabismus #39

  • Classification.
  • b) which eye is deviated
  • alternating strabismus
  • each eye may be alternatively become fixing and deviating eye
  • one eye may fix the switch over to the other occurs spontaneously;
  • monocular strabismus
  • one eye is permanently the fixing eye and the other is always the deviating eye.

Signs: #40

  • primary deviation angle=the secondary one;
  • normal eye movements without limitations In all gaze directions
  • Angle of the optical axes of both eyes remains the same whatever the direction of gaze
  • the disparity in the line of view of the two eyes remains constant in whichever direction they turn;
  • amplyopia with suppressing the binocular vision
  • Should the strabismus become monocular

Symptoms. #41

  • No diplopia
  • although the retinal images are formed on noncorresponding points
  • Antidiplopical mechanisms :
  • a) Pathological neutralization.
  • cortical suppression of the image from the deviating eye
  • inhibition of the image received from the extramacular point;
  • b) Functional amblyopia
  • diminishing visual acuity without an organic ocular lesion
  • a consequence of cortical suppression;

Symptoms. #42

  • c) Abnormal retinal correspondence
  • an attempt to restore a binocular vision
  • a new functional relationship between
  • extramacular point of the deviating eye
  • that takes over the main gaze direction with forwards location
  • the macula of the fixing eye
  • that acquires a secondary visual direction.

Etiology: #43

  • a) Optical factors
  • anisometropia
  • the patient’s two eyes have markedly differing refractive errors;
  • b) Sensorial factors
  • diseases afecting the visual acuity
  • the clear ocular media
  • the retina

Etiology: #44

  • c) Anatomical and motor factors
  • orbit, muscles, ligaments, and nerves
  • d) Innervational factors
  • disturbing the relationship between convergence needed for close work and excessive accommodation (hypermetropia);
  • development anomalies of oculomotor reflexes;
  • disturbances of the supranuclear and cortical innervations
  • weakness of the fusion.

Clinical forms #45

  • Convergent strabismus
  • the most frequently
  • between 2 and 4 years associated mostly with hypermetropia;
  • nasal deviation of the eyeball that accentuates with the age;
  • VA of the strabic
  • decreased
  • lowers as the patient grows-up

Clinical forms #46

  • Divergent strabismus
  • less frequently
  • emerges later, >10 years ;
  • usually connected with myopia
  • may appear in other eyes with decreased VA of pathological causes
  • macular choroiditis,
  • congenital cataract,
  • corneal scars.

Management #47

  • aims
  • removal of the esthetical defect
  • correction of functional disturbances
  • as soon as possible just immediately after diagnosing

Management #48

  • therapeutical steps:
  • Optic treatment
  • Pleoptic treatment
  • Ortoptic treatment
  • Botulinic toxin
  • Surgical treatment
  • Potoperative treatment

Management #49

  • a) Optic treatment ,
  • optical correction of refractive errors ;
  • the great majority of children with convergent strabismus are hypermetropes;
  • total correction of hypermetropia
  • to relax
  • the accommodation
  • the convergence tonus;

Management #50

  • b) Pleoptic treatment
  • treatment of amblyopia ,
  • improvement of vision in each eye by occlusion of the fixing eye
  • forcing the amblyopic eye into use;
  • the strabic eye will take over the fixation
  • inhibition process, (neutralization) suppressed.

Management #51

  • c) Ortoptic treatment
  • establishing or restoring the binocular vision.
  • synoptophor (correction of binocular disturbances)
  • indication
  • heterophories,
  • convergence insufficiency,
  • divergent intermittent strabismus,
  • postoperative treatment for consolidation of the process of healing.
  • d) Botulinic toxin.
  • injection within hypertone muscles with paralyzed effect.

Management #52

  • e) Surgical treatment
  • if ocular deviation persists yet after the first steps
  • the muscle acting in the direction of the deviation is weaken
  • moving insertion backward (recession or retropositioning );
  • the antagonist of this muscle has to be strengthened
  • advancing insertion
  • removal of a small portion of the tendon (resection)

Management #53

  • f) Potoperative treatment
  • ortoptic and/or pleoptic treatment
  • depending upon the status of the visual acuity and binocular vision after straightening the eyeball axes.
